title: New is not the same as *good*.
subtitle: How to judge a ship's age, and when the refit matters more than the launch.

text: A ship refitted well beats a new one designed badly.
sub: Hull age tells you almost nothing on its own. What the last refit actually touched tells you a great deal.

title: Four things a refit either fixed or didn't

items.head: Bathrooms and balconies
items.body: The two places you notice age first, and the two most often left alone to save money.

items.head: Soft goods and lighting
items.body: Cheap to replace, transformative when done. A dated ship is often only a dated palette.

items.head: Public rooms
items.body: A refit that added venues without adding seats has made the crowding worse, not better.

items.head: Engineering and stabilisers
items.body: Never in the press release, always in the ride. Ask before a winter crossing.

title: Where a new ship genuinely pays

points.label: Suite bathrooms
points.value: The biggest improvement in twenty years of ship design. Here, new is worth paying for.

points.label: Balcony proportions
points.value: Newer balconies are deeper and better shaded. Old ones are often a chair and a shin.

points.label: Quiet at speed
points.value: Newer propulsion is noticeably quieter aft, which is where the best suites tend to sit.

points.label: Expedition kit
points.value: Ice class and boat handling have moved on quickly. Older expedition ships show it.

text: Ask what the last refit changed. Not when it happened.
sub: *Refurbished last year* can mean new carpet in the corridors. It can also mean every bathroom aboard. Nobody volunteers which, and both are technically true.

title: Send this to whoever books your holidays
body: Then send me a ship you're considering and I'll tell you what its last refit actually touched.
